questions.stem: What does „der Brauch“ mean, as in „ein alter Brauch“?
options: A brew or a beer
A use or purpose
A ceremony or wedding
A custom or tradition
questions.explanation: „Der Brauch“ is a custom; the plural „Bräuche“ appears in phrases like „Bräuche und Traditionen“. It is related to „brauchen“, but 'use' as a noun is „der Gebrauch“.

questions.stem: Read: „Am 11. November ziehen die Kinder mit selbst gebastelten Laternen durch die Straßen und singen Lieder.“ Which celebration is this?
options: Fasching
Erntedankfest
Sankt Martin
Nikolaustag
questions.explanation: Lantern processions on 11 November mark St Martin's Day, often led by a rider playing Martin. Nikolaustag is 6 December, and „Erntedankfest“ is the harvest festival.

questions.stem: What do children in Germany traditionally do on the evening of 5 December?
options: Walk through the streets with lanterns
Put out a shoe or boot to be filled by St Nicholas
Open the presents that were left under the Christmas tree
Light the first candle on the Advent wreath
questions.explanation: On the night before 6 December, Nikolaustag, children leave a shoe or boot outside the door, and in the morning it holds sweets or small gifts. Presents come on Christmas Eve.

questions.stem: How is the „Adventskranz“ used?
options: One more of its four candles is lit each Sunday of Advent
One of its doors is opened on each day of December
It is hung on the door on Christmas Eve only
All of its candles are lit together on the evening of 6 December
questions.explanation: The Advent wreath has four candles, one for each Sunday before Christmas, so all four are burning on the last one. Opening a door each day is the „Adventskalender“.

questions.stem: What is „die Bescherung“?
options: The Christmas Day church service at midnight
The decorating of the tree in early December
The Christmas market in the town square
The giving of presents, usually on Christmas Eve
questions.explanation: In most German-speaking families presents are exchanged on the evening of 24 December, „Heiligabend“, not on the morning of the 25th as in Australia. The market is the „Weihnachtsmarkt“.

questions.stem: In Austria and Bavaria, who is „der Krampus“?
options: A horned companion of St Nicholas who scares naughty children
A kind elf who helps Father Christmas wrap up all the children's presents
A fairytale giant who guards the mountains in winter
A carnival jester who leads the Rose Monday parade
questions.explanation: The Krampus is St Nicholas's dark companion in the Alpine regions, and „Krampusläufe“, parades of people in Krampus masks, take place in early December. The figure belongs to Advent, not to carnival.

questions.stem: What is „der Rosenmontag“ in the Rhineland?
options: A public holiday marking the end of the harvest
The high point of carnival, with large street parades
A spring festival when couples exchange roses
The first Monday of the long summer school holidays in July
questions.explanation: Rose Monday falls the Monday before Ash Wednesday, and cities such as Köln, Düsseldorf and Mainz hold huge carnival parades. The name has nothing to do with Valentine's Day.

questions.stem: Why do Rhineland carnival clubs gather on 11 November at 11:11?
options: It marks the official start of the carnival season
It marks the anniversary of the end of a war
It marks the day the first ever carnival parade was held in Köln
It marks the last day before the fasting period
questions.explanation: The carnival season opens at 11:11 on the 11th of the 11th, though the parades come months later, just before Lent. Fasting begins on Ash Wednesday, at the end of the season.

questions.stem: What is „die Schultüte“?
options: A school uniform handed out to every child on the first day of each year
A certificate handed to students when they leave school
A cone of sweets and gifts for a child's first day of school
A paper bag used to carry lunch to school each day
questions.explanation: On the day of „Einschulung“, starting primary school, children carry a decorated cone filled with sweets and small gifts. The leaving certificate is „das Abschlusszeugnis“.

questions.stem: What happens at a „Polterabend“?
options: Guests smash crockery before a wedding to bring the couple luck
Families tell ghost stories on the night before All Saints' Day
Friends hold a farewell party before someone moves overseas
Neighbours make loud noise at midnight to welcome the new year
questions.explanation: The „Polterabend“ is held a few days before a wedding, and the couple sweep up the broken china together. „Poltern“ means to clatter or crash.

questions.stem: What is a „Maibaum“?
options: A garland of flowers hung on the door on Mother's Day
A spring market held in the village square throughout the month of May
A decorated pole put up on 1 May, especially in Bavaria and Austria
A fruit tree that flowers in May, planted when a child is born
questions.explanation: The maypole is raised in the village square for 1 May, often decorated with the emblems of local trades. Mother's Day is in May too, but has no maypole.

questions.stem: What does Germany celebrate on 3 October, „Tag der Deutschen Einheit“?
options: The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989
The founding of the Federal Republic of Germany in 1949
The end of the Second World War in 1945
The reunification of East and West Germany in 1990
questions.explanation: Reunification took effect on 3 October 1990, which is why that day, not 9 November, is the national holiday. The Wall fell almost a year earlier, on 9 November 1989.

questions.stem: When is Switzerland's national day?
options: 26 October
1 May
1 August
3 October
questions.explanation: The „Bundesfeier“ on 1 August recalls the alliance of the founding cantons in 1291, with bonfires and fireworks. 26 October is Austria's national day.

questions.stem: What does Austria's national day, 26 October, commemorate?
options: The lifting of the Ottoman siege of the city of Vienna in 1683
The law of 1955 declaring Austria permanently neutral
The founding of the Austrian republic in 1918
Austria's joining of the European Union in 1995
questions.explanation: On 26 October 1955, after the occupying powers had left, Austria's parliament passed the law on permanent neutrality. The First Republic was proclaimed earlier, in November 1918.

questions.stem: What is „ein Märchen“?
options: A legend
A march
A fable
A fairytale
questions.explanation: „Das Märchen“ is a fairytale, such as „Hänsel und Gretel“. A legend tied to a real place is „die Sage“, and a fable with animals and a moral is „die Fabel“.

questions.stem: Who collected and published the „Kinder- und Hausmärchen“, first in 1812?
options: The Brothers Grimm
Hans Christian Andersen
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
questions.explanation: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected folk tales and first published them in 1812. Andersen wrote his own fairytales, in Danish, rather than collecting German ones.

questions.stem: How do German fairytales usually begin?
options: Hier beginnt …
Einmal ist keinmal …
Es war einmal …
Vor langer Zeit gab es …
questions.explanation: „Es war einmal“ is the fixed opening, like 'Once upon a time'. „Einmal ist keinmal“ is a saying meaning 'once doesn't count'.

questions.stem: What does a fairytale's closing line „Und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, dann leben sie noch heute“ correspond to in English?
options: And they all died long ago
And they lived happily ever after
And that was the end of them
And nobody ever saw them again
questions.explanation: Literally 'and if they have not died, they are still living today', it is the German formula for a happy ending. A literal reading makes it sound gloomier than it is.

questions.stem: Who is „Rotkäppchen“?
options: Sleeping Beauty
Cinderella
Little Red Riding Hood
Snow White
questions.explanation: „Rot“ is red and „Käppchen“ a little cap. Snow White is „Schneewittchen“, Sleeping Beauty „Dornröschen“ and Cinderella „Aschenputtel“.

questions.stem: What is the legend of the Loreley?
options: A giant who threw rocks into the Rhine to make its rapids
A maiden on a Rhine cliff whose song lures boatmen to their deaths
A dragon in the Rhine that was killed by a knight called Siegfried
A piper who led the children of a town away into a mountain
questions.explanation: The Loreley rock stands at a narrow, dangerous bend of the Rhine, and Heinrich Heine's poem made the siren famous. The piper belongs to Hameln, and the dragon to the Nibelungen.

questions.stem: In the legend of the „Rattenfänger von Hameln“, why does the piper lead the children away?
options: The town refused to pay him for ridding it of rats
The children had laughed at his music in the square
The town had asked him to take them to a new school
A witch had ordered him to bring her the town's children
questions.explanation: The Pied Piper of Hamelin played the rats into the river, was cheated of his fee, and took the children in revenge. The story is a „Sage“, tied to a real town in Lower Saxony.

questions.stem: In which city was Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart born?
options: Munich
Salzburg
Vienna
Bonn
questions.explanation: Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756 and later worked in Vienna. Bonn is Beethoven's birthplace, which is the usual swap.

questions.stem: In which city was Ludwig van Beethoven born?
options: Bonn
Vienna
Salzburg
Leipzig
questions.explanation: Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770 and spent most of his working life in Vienna, which is why the two cities both claim him. Leipzig is associated with Bach.

questions.stem: Which work is Johann Wolfgang von Goethe best known for?
options: Die Zauberflöte
Die Blechtrommel
Faust
Die Räuber
questions.explanation: Goethe's „Faust“ is the best-known work of German literature. „Die Räuber“ is by his friend Schiller, „Die Zauberflöte“ is Mozart's opera and „Die Blechtrommel“ is Günter Grass's novel.

questions.stem: What was the „Bauhaus“, founded in Weimar in 1919?
options: A museum of German history in the house where Goethe lived
A school of art, design and architecture that shaped modern design
A building company that rebuilt German cities after the Second World War
A political party that governed the Weimar Republic in the 1920s
questions.explanation: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus to join art and craft, and its plain, functional style shaped furniture and buildings worldwide. It later moved to Dessau and then Berlin.

questions.stem: What did Johannes Gutenberg develop in Mainz around 1450?
options: Printing with movable metal type
The first German dictionary
The first public postal service
A translation of the Bible into German
questions.explanation: Gutenberg's press made books far cheaper to produce, beginning with his printed Bible. The famous German translation of the Bible came later, from Martin Luther.

questions.stem: Why is Martin Luther important to the German language?
options: He founded the first German-speaking university
He invented the German letter ß
His translation of the Bible helped set a common written German
He wrote the first grammar book of the German language for schools
questions.explanation: Luther translated the New Testament into German in 1522 and the whole Bible by 1534, and printing spread his language across the German-speaking lands. He is also known for his 95 theses of 1517, which began the Reformation.

questions.stem: In which year was the Berlin Wall built?
questions.explanation: East Germany sealed the border through Berlin on 13 August 1961. 1949 is when the two German states were founded, and 1989 is when the Wall fell.

questions.stem: Who was Sophie Scholl?
options: An East German athlete who won Olympic gold medals
A writer whose diary of years in hiding in Amsterdam became famous
A scientist who discovered nuclear fission in Berlin
A student in the „Weiße Rose“ group that resisted the Nazis
questions.explanation: Sophie Scholl and her brother Hans spread leaflets against the Nazi regime in Munich and were executed in 1943. The diary from Amsterdam is Anne Frank's.

questions.stem: What are „Stolpersteine“, found in the pavements of many German-speaking cities?
options: Plaques marking the houses where famous composers lived
Small brass plaques naming victims of Nazism outside their former homes
Uneven paving stones that survive from the medieval centre of the old town
Stones marking the line where the Berlin Wall once stood
questions.explanation: „Stolpern“ is to stumble: the artist Gunter Demnig began laying the plaques in the 1990s so that passers-by 'stumble' on a name. They are a clear case of the past shaping the present.

questions.stem: In which city was Albert Einstein born?
options: Ulm
Berlin
Zürich
Bern
questions.explanation: Einstein was born in Ulm in 1879. He later worked at the patent office in Bern, studied in Zürich and taught in Berlin, which is why all three are linked with him.

questions.stem: Where would you most expect to be greeted with „Grüß Gott“?
options: In Berlin
In Luxembourg
In Bavaria or Austria
In Hamburg or Bremen
questions.explanation: „Grüß Gott“ is the standard greeting in southern Germany and Austria. In northern Germany you are more likely to hear „Moin“.

questions.stem: What is „Grüezi“?
options: A Bavarian toast
A northern German thank-you
A Swiss German greeting
An Austrian farewell
questions.explanation: „Grüezi“ is the polite greeting in much of German-speaking Switzerland, used with people you would address as „Sie“. Friends tend to say „Hoi“.

questions.stem: In Bavaria and Austria, what does „Servus“ mean?
options: Hello or goodbye, between people who know each other
Thank you, after being served in a restaurant
Cheers, when raising a glass to someone
Excuse me, when pushing past in a crowd
questions.explanation: „Servus“, from Latin 'your servant', is an informal greeting and farewell in the south. A toast is „Prost“, and 'excuse me' is „Entschuldigung“.

questions.stem: How does written Swiss Standard German differ from the German of Germany and Austria?
options: It uses French spelling for verbs
It does not use the letter ß
It does not capitalise nouns
It has no genitive case
questions.explanation: Switzerland writes „ss“ wherever Germany and Austria write ß: „die Strasse“, not „die Straße“. Nouns are capitalised in Swiss Standard German as everywhere else.

questions.stem: What is „die Marille“ in Austria?
options: An apricot
A plum
A potato
A tomato
questions.explanation: Austrian German has many food words of its own: „die Marille“ for the „Aprikose“ of Germany. A potato can be „Erdapfel“ and a tomato „Paradeiser“.

questions.stem: In Bavaria and Austria, what is „eine Semmel“?
options: A type of sausage
A semolina pudding
A beer mug
A bread roll
questions.explanation: The bread roll has many regional names: „Brötchen“ in much of Germany, „Semmel“ in the south and Austria, „Schrippe“ in Berlin. A litre of beer in Bavaria is „eine Maß“.

questions.stem: Which South Australian town was founded in 1839 by Prussian Lutheran settlers?
options: Bendigo
Mildura
Hahndorf
Ballarat
questions.explanation: Hahndorf in the Adelaide Hills was named after Captain Dirk Hahn, who brought the settlers out on the ship „Zebra“. Ballarat and Bendigo are Victorian gold-rush towns.

questions.stem: Why did many of the first German settlers in South Australia leave Prussia in the 1830s?
options: They were miners recruited for the goldfields that had just been found
They were fleeing the fighting of the First World War in Europe
They were soldiers who were given land as a reward for service in the British army
They were Lutherans who rejected the church union imposed by the Prussian king
questions.explanation: The Old Lutherans resisted the forced union of the Lutheran and Reformed churches, and Pastor August Kavel led groups to South Australia from 1838. The gold rushes began only in 1851.

questions.stem: Which wine region in South Australia was largely settled by German-speaking Lutherans from the 1840s?
options: The Barossa Valley
The Hunter Valley
The Yarra Valley
The Margaret River region
questions.explanation: The Barossa still has Lutheran churches, German place names and bakeries selling „Streuselkuchen“. The Hunter is in New South Wales and the Yarra Valley in Victoria.

questions.stem: What happened to many German place names in South Australia during the First World War?
options: They were protected by a law that banned renaming
They were kept, but only on German-language maps
Dozens were officially changed to non-German names
They were all translated word for word into English
questions.explanation: A 1917 law renamed dozens of places, using English, war-related and Aboriginal names, so Hahndorf became Ambleside for a time. Some, Hahndorf among them, were restored in the 1930s, while many others never were.

questions.stem: Who was Ludwig Leichhardt?
options: A German botanist who founded the Sydney Botanic Garden
A Lutheran pastor who led the first settlers to Hahndorf
A German composer who wrote a symphony about the Australian bush
A Prussian explorer who vanished in inland Australia in 1848
questions.explanation: Leichhardt led an expedition from Moreton Bay to Port Essington in 1844–45 and disappeared on a later attempt to cross the continent. The pastor who led settlers was Kavel.

questions.stem: Who were the „Gastarbeiter“ in West Germany from the 1950s?
options: Hotel staff who worked in the tourist industry
Students from abroad who worked part-time during their studies
Workers recruited from countries such as Italy and Turkey
Germans who worked abroad and later returned home
questions.explanation: West Germany signed recruitment agreements with Italy in 1955 and Turkey in 1961, among others. Many workers stayed, which is why the migration experience is part of the theme.
